newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba, South Africa sign trade accord.
newsitem.headline: Cuba, South Africa sign trade accord.

text.p: Cuba and South Africa have signed a bilateral trade accord, marking the latest step in a diplomatic relationship which has irked Washington.
The trade accord was signed during a two-day visit by South African Trade Minister Alec Erwin and a 20-member trade delegation that ended late on Tuesday.
Erwin told reporters at Havana airport he saw considerable opportunities for South African companies in Cuba. He said the trade accord included giving mutual most favoured nation status.
During his visit, he met Cuban government ministers including Trade Minister Ricardo Cabrisas, Basic Industries Minister Marcos Portal and Transport Minister Alvaro Perez Morales.
On Tuesday evening, he met President Fidel Castro, whom has been repeatedly invited to visit South Africa by President Nelson Mandela.
Mandela, who established diplomatic ties with Cuba the day after his May 10, 1994 inauguration, has called Cuba "a good friend."
He has resisted U.S. pressure to cool his relations with Cuba, saying he will not dump those who supported his African National Congress during its exile from white-ruled South Africa.
During Erwin's visit, a letter of intent was also signed during the visit for the supply of equipment to the Cuban sugar industry, but details were not available.
South African interest in Cuba includes mining, sugar and transport. Bilateral trade between the two countries was worth $35 million last year.

The trade balance is heavily in South Africa's favour, consisting mostly of South African exports of agro-chemicals, although Erwin said South Africa was interested in possible future imports of Cuban medical products.
Cape-Town based firm Atlantis Diesel Engines (ADE) has an $80 million contract to supply Cuba with 10,000 diesel engines.

The two nations have an investment promotion and protection accord, as well as health and education cooperation agreements. About 450 Cuban doctors arrived in South Africa last year to work in rural and township hospitals.

Last August in Havana, visiting South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said South Africa had expressed opposition to the U.S. Helms-Burton measure tightening the economic embargo in Cuba, and termed it "a bad law."
